plan.topic: Starting orforglipron (Foundayo), the once-daily GLP-1 pill approved in the US for chronic weight management: what to expect in the first weeks and months, from the US prescribing information (rev 7/2026) and Medication Guide only. This is the fixed re-render of the verified script that was held on 11-11 and got a REVISE on 11-20 (playbook queue #4).
plan.angle: Run the locked label-only script exactly as described, with every 11-20 and 11-11 fix applied. Change the thumbnail headline from 'FIRST MONTH?' to 'STARTING THE PILL?', with the subtext 'orforglipron (Foundayo), US label', a pill bottle and one calm labelled character. Keep the working title, or use 'Starting Orforglipron (Foundayo): What the US Label Says to Expect'. The only time wording in the video should be the label's GI timing line ('mostly during dose escalation and decreased over time'). Don't promise or describe a week-by-week or month-by-month timeline. For NAION, quote the live Foundayo PI if the new warning is printed there. Otherwise use 'In November 2026 the FDA asked all GLP-1 medicine labels to add a warning about a rare eye condition called NAION', citing the FDA's own 9 Nov 2026 Drug Safety Communication page. Include the Canada/TGA description line only if Health Canada's and the TGA's own pages confirm both approvals and dates. Otherwise leave it out.
plan.why: Next ready item in the playbook's long-video queue, with the 11-20 fact-check fixes already listed. It's an approved-drug search format with proven drug-name search ('foundayo': 27 searches, 468 minutes). Canada and Australia approvals add live demand, and it rests only on the label, which keeps fact-check risk low. | fact-check: Safe and on-brand. It is a label-only explainer of a US-approved prescription GLP-1 pill. It has no dosing, titration, missed-dose, switching or sourcing advice, and the 11-20 REVISE fixes and 11-11 render fixes are already built in. Checks done: (1) NAION: the FDA announced the class-wide requirement on 9 Nov 2026, adding NAION to Warnings and Precautions for all GLP-1 RAs. The fallback wording is accurate. The fact-checker should still confirm whether the live Foundayo PI has been updated before quoting it, and must cite the FDA DSC page itself, not news coverage. (2) Health Canada: news reports (CTV, CP24, Global News) say Foundayo was authorized on 13 Nov 2026, but I have not confirmed this on Health Canada's own page. I found no confirmation of a TGA approval or date. Keep the angle's rule: drop the line unless both are confirmed on the regulators' own pages. Also, the Canadian product reportedly includes a type 2 diabetes use, so the 'check your local leaflet' wording is needed if the line ships. (3) Packaging risk: the 'FIRST MONTH?' thumbnail and the 'first weeks and months' topic promise a timeline. The script can't give one because it has no titration talk, and the label's only timing wording is about GI effects (mostly during dose escalation, decreasing over time). That breaks the rule against promising a timeframe the video doesn't give. Change the thumbnail headline. (4) Dose numbers: the 17.2 mg top label dose and the 36 mg trial arm may appear on stat cards only as arm labels, never spoken and never framed as a recommendation. Keep 'averages, not predictions' on the results cards.

script.hook_pattern: Visceral 'you' scenario folded into sentence 1, then answer-first (Exp H). The label's GI timing line comes by about 12 s: nausea, vomiting and diarrhea were more common during dose escalation and decreased over time. A second concrete payoff (top-trial-dose average versus placebo) lands at 15–30 s, and one open loop (the family-history question) pays off in the family-history chapter.

scenes.narration: You're about to start orforglipron, the Foundayo pill, and wondering what to expect? Here's what the US label says.

visual.stock_query: calm woman holding pill bottle, curious

scenes.retention_device: Drug-first question in 'you' terms; first frame matches the spoken words

scenes.narration: The short answer: most of the common adverse reactions are gut ones, like nausea. And the label says nausea, vomiting and diarrhea were more common while the dose was being stepped up, and decreased over time.

items: Most common: mostly gut effects, like nausea
Nausea, vomiting, diarrhea: higher during escalation

scenes.retention_device: Answer delivered by about 12 s, in the label's exact scope

scenes.narration: Second, the results. In the main seventy-two-week trial, in adults with obesity, or overweight plus a weight-related condition, and without diabetes, the top trial dose did the most.
scenes.retention_device: Second concrete payoff set up at 15–30 s

scenes.narration: Average weight loss: eleven point two percent. On placebo: two point one percent.

visual.stat_label: Orforglipron avg weight loss, 72 wks, top trial dose vs placebo; adults with obesity or overweight + weight-related condition, no diabetes (ATTAIN-1)
visual.stock_query: two bars on a chart, celebrating

scenes.narration: Those are averages, not predictions. Yours could be more, or less.

visual.stock_query: spread of dots around average line

scenes.narration: And before your very first pill, there's one family-history question the label puts front and center. I'll get to it.

visual.stock_query: family photo frame with question mark

scenes.retention_device: Main open loop (paid off in 'The family question')

scenes.narration: So what exactly is in that bottle, and why is it a pill instead of a shot?

visual.stock_query: curious woman peering into pill bottle

scenes.narration: Orforglipron is a GLP-one receptor agonist. It acts on the same receptor as GLP-one, a hormone your gut releases after you eat.
Here's the twist. Injected GLP-one medicines like semaglutide are peptides, chains of amino acids. Orforglipron isn't. It's a small, non-peptide molecule, and it comes as a once-daily tablet.

visual.stock_query: tiny pill beside long bead chain

scenes.narration: So it's not a version of the semaglutide pill. It's a different molecule, tested in its own trials.

visual.myth: It's just the semaglutide pill again
visual.fact: A different molecule, with its own trials
visual.stock_query: two different pills side by side

scenes.narration: Imagine Dana, fifty-two, holding her first bottle at the kitchen counter. She's relieved there's no needle. She's also nervous, because her sister felt queasy on a weekly shot.

visual.stock_query: Dana at kitchen counter, pill bottle, nervous smile

scenes.narration: Hopeful and uneasy at once? Both make sense, and the label speaks to both.
scenes.retention_device: Names and validates the feeling, promises answers

scenes.narration: For some people, a daily tablet simply feels easier to start than an injection. That's a personal preference, and a fair one to raise with your prescriber.
scenes.on_screen_text: A fair thing to ask about

scenes.narration: So who is Foundayo actually approved for?
In the US, it's approved to reduce excess body weight and keep it off long term, in adults with obesity, or adults with overweight plus at least one weight-related condition.

items: Reduce weight and keep it off long term

scenes.retention_device: Concrete answer to the chapter question

scenes.narration: It goes alongside a reduced-calorie diet and increased physical activity. Think of the pill as one part of the plan, not the whole plan.

visual.stock_query: pill, vegetables and walking shoes together

scenes.retention_device: Analogy: one piece of a puzzle

scenes.narration: It's a prescription medicine, so your prescriber weighs your whole health picture first. Talk to your doctor or prescriber about whether it's right for you.
scenes.on_screen_text: Ask if it's right for you

visual.stock_query: doctor and patient reviewing chart together

scenes.narration: But the label also lists people who shouldn't take it at all, and one of them comes down to your family tree. Hold that thought.
First, the question Dana really wants answered: what might this actually do for me?
scenes.on_screen_text: What might it do for me?

scenes.narration: How much weight did people lose, and how many stopped?
In the ATTAIN one trial, just over three thousand adults with obesity, or overweight plus a weight-related condition, and without diabetes, took orforglipron or placebo for seventy-two weeks.
scenes.retention_device: Population and design in one sentence, no setup scene

scenes.narration: The US label reports this study as its Trial One, in adults without diabetes.
scenes.retention_device: Credibility link from trial to label

scenes.narration: The trial used a different tablet form, so its doses have different numbers. The label lists its top dose as seventeen point two milligrams. On that dose, the label reports an average loss of eleven point one percent, versus two point one percent on placebo.

visual.stat_label: Foundayo avg weight loss, label Trial 1, 72 wks: 17.2 mg vs placebo; adults without diabetes
visual.stock_query: Dana comparing label page and trial chart

scenes.retention_device: Clears up the trial-versus-label dose numbers

scenes.narration: Remember the trial's top-dose average? Eleven point two percent. That's roughly one ninth of body weight. On placebo, two point one percent. About one fiftieth.

visual.stat_label: Avg body weight lost: top trial dose vs placebo

scenes.retention_device: Payoff callback with a humanised comparison

scenes.narration: The two lower trial doses averaged smaller losses than the top dose.
But averages hide a spread. In any trial, some people lose more than the average, and some lose less.
Here's the number a lot of videos skip. How many people stopped because of adverse events?
On the top trial dose, ten point three percent stopped because of adverse events. On placebo, two point six percent.

visual.stat_label: Orforglipron, ATTAIN-1, 72 wks: stopped for adverse events, top trial dose vs placebo

scenes.narration: Flip that around: about nine in ten on the top trial dose didn't stop because of adverse events. People also left the trial for other reasons, so overall dropout was higher.

visual.stock_query: ten cartoon people, one stepping aside

scenes.narration: For Dana, that's the honest picture: real average results, and a real chance her stomach complains while her dose is being stepped up. So what does that look like, and what helps?
What do the gut effects look like, and do they last?
In ATTAIN one, the most common adverse events were gastrointestinal, like nausea, and they were mostly mild to moderate.

items: Most common: gut effects, like nausea

scenes.narration: And a tablet isn't automatically gentler. Even as a pill, the trial's most common adverse events were still gut ones.

visual.myth: A pill means no gut effects
visual.fact: Gut effects were still the most common

scenes.narration: The label's timing line is the one to remember. Nausea, vomiting and diarrhea were more common during dose escalation, and decreased over time.
Dose escalation simply means the stretch when your dose is being stepped up, on the plan your prescriber sets. No guessing, and no changes on your own.
That's not a promise about any single day. But it's a pattern worth knowing on the morning you feel off and wonder if it's forever.
So what helps? The NHS suggests a few simple things for feeling sick.
Eat smaller, more frequent meals. Take regular sips of a cold drink. And skip hot, fried or greasy food.

items: Regular sips of a cold drink
Skip hot, fried or greasy food

scenes.narration: Keep up your fluids, unless you've been told to limit fluids. The label notes that diarrhea, nausea and vomiting may cause a loss of fluids, which may cause kidney problems.
The label says to tell your healthcare provider right away if you have nausea, vomiting or diarrhea that does not go away. That's useful information, not complaining.
scenes.on_screen_text: Gut effects won't go away? Tell provider right away
scenes.retention_device: Agency and permission, with the label's action line

scenes.narration: Picture Dana at her desk, a little queasy after lunch. She swaps to a smaller plate, sips something cold, and makes a note to mention it at her next check-in.

visual.stock_query: Dana at desk, small plate, cold drink

scenes.narration: One sign is different: severe pain in your stomach area that won't go away, with or without nausea or vomiting, sometimes felt through to your back. The label says stop taking it and call your healthcare provider right away. For anything that isn't one of those emergency signs, don't stop or change your medicine on your own.
scenes.on_screen_text: Severe pain that won't go away

items: Severe stomach pain that won't go away
Stop taking it, call right away
Non-emergency: don't stop or change alone
visual.stock_query: person calling doctor, calm and focused

scenes.retention_device: Warning sign and action in one payoff scene; goes straight to the next chapter question

scenes.narration: So what's the family-history question I promised?
The label says don't take orforglipron if you or anyone in your family has ever had a thyroid cancer called medullary thyroid carcinoma, or MTC.
And don't take it if you have an endocrine condition called MEN two.
scenes.retention_device: Exact label terms on a big card

scenes.narration: That's why your prescriber asks about your family, not only you. Not sure? Ask your relatives before the appointment.
The label also says to tell your healthcare provider if you get a lump or swelling in your neck, hoarseness, trouble swallowing, or shortness of breath.
scenes.on_screen_text: Neck lump or hoarseness? Tell provider

items: Lump or swelling in your neck
visual.stock_query: person touching neck, calm doctor nearby

scenes.narration: There's more to mention up front, and one item is about diabetes medicines you might already take.
If you also take a medicine that can cause low blood sugar, such as insulin or a sulfonylurea, the label says your risk of low blood sugar may be higher.
scenes.on_screen_text: Insulin or sulfonylurea? Low-sugar risk may be higher

visual.stock_query: insulin pen and pill box on table

scenes.narration: The label also reports low blood sugar in some adults without type 2 diabetes in its Trial One. So bring a list of every medicine you take.
scenes.on_screen_text: Low sugar also reported without type 2 diabetes
scenes.retention_device: Completes the scope, turns it into one action

scenes.narration: Gallbladder problems are listed too. Signs include pain in your upper stomach, fever, yellowing of your skin or eyes, or clay-colored stools. Tell your healthcare provider right away.
scenes.on_screen_text: Gallbladder signs? Tell provider right away

scenes.narration: If you have signs of a serious allergic reaction, call your local emergency number, like nine one one, nine nine nine or triple zero, right away, and stop taking it. Signs include swelling of your face, lips, tongue or throat; trouble breathing or swallowing; severe rash or itching; fainting or feeling dizzy; and a very rapid heartbeat.
scenes.on_screen_text: Allergy signs: call emergency right away, stop taking it

items: Swelling of face, lips, tongue or throat

scenes.retention_device: Emergency number first, full label sign list

scenes.narration: For anything that isn't one of those emergency signs, don't stop or change your medicine on your own.
scenes.on_screen_text: Non-emergency: don't stop or change alone

scenes.narration: One line of context. The FDA is requiring makers of all GLP-one receptor agonist medicines to add a warning to their labels about a possible higher risk of a rare eye condition called NAION. If you notice sudden vision loss, especially in one eye, or other vision changes, contact your healthcare professional right away.
scenes.on_screen_text: FDA: NAION warning for GLP-1 class labels

visual.stock_query: calm eye doctor with eye chart

scenes.retention_device: One neutral sentence of context, plus a clear action

scenes.narration: Dana writes three things on a sticky note: any family history of MTC or MEN two, her full medicine list, and the warning signs. That's the homework.
scenes.retention_device: Thread callback turns warnings into agency

scenes.narration: That's the hard part done. The rest is about making the pill fit your life.
scenes.retention_device: Relief beat bridging to the next chapter

scenes.narration: Once you've started, what helps you get the most from it?
Start with the label's own frame: a reduced-calorie diet and increased physical activity, with the pill alongside.
scenes.retention_device: Callback to 'one part of the plan'

scenes.narration: When you're eating less, make protein a priority. Ask your care team for a protein target that fits you, and build meals around it.
scenes.on_screen_text: Protein first, target from your team

scenes.narration: Ask whether strength training fits your plan, to look after your muscle as your weight changes. Simple bodyweight moves can be a start.
Eat slowly, and notice when you feel comfortably full. You don't have to finish the plate.
And track more than the scale. Energy, sleep, blood pressure and how far you can walk are health signals too.
scenes.retention_device: Reframe: weight is one measure among many

scenes.narration: Here's the whole video in three lines.
One. Most of the common adverse reactions are gut ones, like nausea. Nausea, vomiting and diarrhea were more common during dose escalation, and decreased over time.

Two. In the main seventy-two-week trial, in adults with obesity, or overweight plus a weight-related condition, without diabetes, the top trial dose did the most. Eleven point two percent average weight loss. Two point one percent on placebo. Averages, not predictions.
Three. Before you start, tell your prescriber about any personal or family history of MTC or MEN two, and every medicine you take.

items: Personal or family MTC or MEN 2

scenes.narration: Dana walks into her appointment with her sticky note. She isn't certain about everything, but she's clear on what to ask. That's the goal for you, too.

visual.stock_query: Dana confident in clinic waiting room

scenes.narration: Talk to your doctor or prescriber about whether Foundayo is right for you.
scenes.on_screen_text: Ask if it's right for you

factcheck.summary:
This needs one real fix before it ships. The placebo figure for people who stopped because of adverse events is wrong in s28: the ATTAIN-1 abstract on PubMed and Europe PMC says 2.7%, not 2.6%. The 10.3% for the top trial dose is correct.

Everything else I checked matches its source:
- **Trial results:** 3,127 adults, 72 weeks, average weight loss of 11.2% on the top trial dose (36 mg) vs 2.1% on placebo, smaller losses on the lower doses, and gut effects the most common adverse events, mostly mild to moderate.
- **Label (revised 7/2026):** the approved use (including keeping weight off long term), the line that nausea, vomiting and diarrhea were higher while the dose was stepped up and decreased over time, 11.1% vs 2.1% on 17.2 mg in Trial 1, the MTC or MEN 2 warning, low blood sugar in Trial 1 adults without type 2 diabetes (0.6% vs 0% on placebo), and the trial's different tablet form.
- **Medication Guide (issued 07/2026):** the thyroid, gallbladder, fluids and "nausea, vomiting or diarrhea that does not go away" lines, and the low blood sugar line with insulin or a sulfonylurea.
- **NHS nausea page:** reviewed 17 Nov 2023, and the three tips match.
- **FDA NAION bulletin:** dated 9 Nov 2026, real and accurately summarised.

The Dana scenes are clearly hypothetical and fine as written. There are also two small wording fixes, in s42 and s54.

issues.claim: On placebo, two point six percent [stopped because of adverse events]; stat 10.3% vs 2.6%
issues.problem: The ATTAIN-1 NEJM abstract reports that 2.7% stopped because of adverse events on placebo, not 2.6%. The 10.3% on 36 mg is correct.
issues.fix: Narration: "On the top trial dose, ten point three percent stopped because of adverse events. On placebo, two point seven percent." stat_value: "10.3% vs 2.7%". Also correct 2.6% to 2.7% in the description, pinned comment and any caption.

issues.claim: severe pain in your stomach area that won't go away, with or without nausea or vomiting
issues.problem: Adding "nausea" goes beyond the Medication Guide's pancreatitis wording. Channel rule: keep "with or without vomiting" word for word.
issues.fix: "One sign is different: severe pain in your stomach area that won't go away, with or without vomiting. You may feel the pain from your stomach area to your back. The label says stop taking it and call your healthcare provider right away. For anything that isn't one of those emergency signs, don't stop or change your medicine on your own."

issues.claim: The FDA is requiring makers of all GLP-one receptor agonist medicines to add a warning…
issues.problem: "Is requiring" will go out of date (evergreen rule). The FDA bulletin also says "potential" increased risk and advises contacting a provider promptly.
issues.fix: "One line of context. The FDA has required makers of GLP-one receptor agonist medicines to add a warning to their labels about a potential higher risk of a rare eye condition called NAION. If you notice sudden vision loss, especially in one eye, or other vision changes, contact your healthcare provider right away."
